notes: Shared Windows prerequisites stored in msvc-redist/, dotnet-framework/ and deps/. These folders have no download plans, so `match` here differs from the other install.json files: it is {"folder": "<top-level folder>", "file": "<filename glob>", "arch": ..., "versions": ...} instead of catalogue os/kind/format fields. Recipes whose file glob matches nothing stored today (VC++ 2005-2013 standalone redists) are research-only entries for files the operator may add later; they say so in `notes`. Everything that installs system-wide is `isolation: "leaks"` by design: the VC++ runtime and .NET Framework are serviced by Windows Update and shared by every program. Where Microsoft documents an app-local alternative (copying the CRT DLLs next to the runtime's own executable) a separate `method: "extract"` recipe gives it with `isolation: "full"`; the installer picks one per app. `uninstall` for shared components is deliberately 'do not uninstall': another app (or the OS) may depend on them. Nothing here was run: this Linux host has no Windows, and the test VMs were off limits, so every recipe is `tested: false`; facts marked 'verified against the stored file' came from reading the files read-only (7-Zip listings, WiX Burn manifests, the 7z-SFX config block, PE import tables).

recipes.notes: App-local ('local') deployment is documented and supported by Microsoft: the DLLs go in the SAME folder as the executable that loads them (for a runtime like Python that is the folder holding python.exe, not the app's own folder). Two apps each get their own copy, so this is the per-app answer to the system-wide redist. Caveats from Microsoft: app-local copies are not serviced by Windows Update; on Windows 10/11 the system UCRT is always used even if a local copy exists; before Windows 8 an app-local UCRT only works next to the main exe, not next to a plugin DLL in another folder. Microsoft's redistribution terms allow redistributing these files; the operator should still confirm the licence for shipping them from our mirror. The build-time extraction step is not a base-installer 'unpack' (Burn is not zip/7z); alternatively take the same DLLs from a VS install's VC\Redist\MSVC\<ver>\<arch>\Microsoft.VC143.CRT folder.

Switches, verified from the SFX config: /ai quiet, all packages (runs 'Installer.cmd /quiet'); /gm2 hides the extraction dialog; /y passive with progress; /aiA quiet + hide ARP entries; /aiV VC++ only (no VSTOR / VB extras); /ai5 /ai8 /aiX /ai2 /ai3 /ai9 install only 2005 / 2008 / 2010 / 2012 / 2013 / 2015-2019 and combine (e.g. /aiX239); /aiT VSTOR only; /aiE extras only; /aiC passive without the UCRT; /aiR auto-uninstall everything; /aiD debug log to the Desktop without installing. The single-version switches run msiexec on the bundled MSIs directly with '/qn /norestart' and skip the removal pass. /ai is what the operator's tested XP/Vista setup uses; consider '/ai9 /gm2' (2015-2019 only) when an app needs just vcruntime140, to shrink the blast radius. It is a third-party repackaging of Microsoft files, which is a licence and supply-chain question for the operator; the SHA-256 in TESTED-WINDOWS.md should be checked before running it.

The {runtime_dir} destination must be the folder holding the runtime's main .exe (see the msvc-redist app-local recipe for the rules). Microsoft documents that app-local UCRT on XP works the same as on other versions, and that XP needs a redist no newer than 14.27 officially; these 14.28.29213 DLLs import no post-XP APIs, and are what the operator's tested XP Python runs on after /ai, but app-local use of them has not been tested on XP. For VC++ 2010/2012/2013 the same pattern works from 2010\x86\Win\System, 2012\x86\Win\System and 2013\x86\System (msvcr100/110/120.dll + msvcp*.dll; no manifests needed from 2010 on). 2005/2008 are WinSxS assemblies: app-local needs the private-assembly form (the Microsoft.VC80.CRT / Microsoft.VC90.CRT folder with its manifest next to the exe), and machine-wide publisher policy can still redirect to a newer system copy.

recipes.notes: System-wide by nature: there is exactly one .NET Framework 4.x per machine, so two versions side by side, or a private copy, is impossible (hence `impossible`, not `leaks`). Exit codes (same for all 4.x installers): 0 success; 3010 success, reboot required; 1641 success, reboot initiated; 1602 cancelled; 1603 fatal error; 5100 system requirements not met. With /norestart the installer must read the exit code and tell the user to reboot on 3010. Optional: /ChainingPackage <name> for Microsoft's telemetry, /passive /showrmui to let the user close running .NET apps. Not for Windows 7/8.1/early 10 (use a 4.8 installer, not stored) and not for XP (max 4.0) or Vista (max 4.6).
